Each fall, the Roger Ebert Fellowship program selects three College of Media undergraduate students at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to participate in a yearlong fellowship that aims to shape their skills in critical writing through immersion in the film industry. The Roger Ebert Fellows for the 2026-27 academic year are media and cinema studies students Ciel Baptiste, Ali Kilmek, and Kris Modi.This festival dispatch from the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival was authored by Klimek, who attended screenings and events in her capacity as a fellow.
p

In his latest film, director Ira Sachs orchestrates a vulnerable, soulful account of queerness in all its beauty, danger, eroticism, and performance. Following a locally celebrated cabaret performer, Jimmy George (Rami Malek), as he returns from an extended hospital stay to his New York City apartment alongside partner and caretaker Dennis (Tom Sturridge), “The Man I Love” looks on as George jumps back into his theatrical, hedonistic lifestyle while faced with a newfound AIDS diagnosis.
p

Sachs (who on Tuesday introduced the film’s Chicago International Film Festival screening, participated in a post-film conversation, and was presented with the festival’s Q-Hugo Artistic Achievement Award) here brings to life a story that on the surface deals with illness—and, as Sachs reflected in the post-screening Q&A, that deals with “a man who couldn’t remember his lines.” Yet, at its core, “The Man I Love” is a far richer tale of human mortality and an enticing exploration of the individual’s indomitable spirit, with Jimmy George formidably embodying this idea.
p

Throughout his journey as a queer man struggling amid the AIDS epidemic of the 1980s, he never feels like a patient defined by his illness; Malek delivers a transformative performance that instead complicates this protagonist, showcasing all the areas of humanity we are often quick to ignore and sweep under the rug for comfort’s sake. In particular, Jimmy’s lustful relationship with upstairs neighbor Vincent (Luther Ford)—which escalates quickly, as he recuperates, from an initial attraction into a torrid, barely concealed affair—reflects these less sympathetic, perhaps less positive, and yet undeniably still alluring attributes of Jimmy’s life: those reckless impulses that keep the anima alive and exhilarated.
p

Sachs described the development of this character, and of Malek’s performance, as “a concentration in making the film on all the things I would miss when I was dead: light, cinema, sex, skin, emotion, and pain.” The tension his protagonist represents—between selfishly indulging in worldly pleasures and acknowledging the reality of a worsening condition—drew tears from many in our audience through its raw, honest depiction of how flawed characters navigate complicated relationships while contending with what they truly believe to be love.
p

Sachs frames love in such interestingly intense ways within the film, the only seemingly unconditional kind coming from Dennis and Jimmy’s sister, Brenda (Rebecca Hall). All of the other characters’ love for Jimmy, we discover, is motivated by something larger than life: admiration, awe, and attraction. (Vincent, with his outsized view of Jimmy, represents all three.) In their affair, the two men walk the line of the classic “artist and muse” trope; though Jimmy initially claims to be interested in Vincent artistically, rather than carnally, this catalyst is soon proven ephemeral and just as swiftly abandoned. It’s in these moments between characters Sachs’ directorial talent is most apparent. The way the scenes exercise a certain restraint when approaching such calculated, cliché beats brings out a sense of slow-brewing empathy from both other characters and the audience—not through an overbearing score or theatrics, but through the nuances of body language and immersion in naturalistic staging. The texture of these performances—and of quiet, small moments between characters—always communicates to us as the audience exactly what we need to understand without blatantly spelling out what we should feel as a result.
p

The score as a whole is additionally meticulous; the film takes its title from a 1924 song composed by George Gershwin for the Broadway musical Lady, Be Good!, which Jimmy performs in a fiery moment at a drag cabaret. For Sachs, conceptualizing where to integrate musical numbers and performance art into “The Man I Love” was a delicate process, as he reflected during the post-film Q&A. “There’s usually a mention of ‘there will be a song performed here’ [in the script], but primarily those are spaces that in the making of the film I slowly try to fill,” Sachs explained. “It’s really something that hits me as another layer of experience of directing, which is figuring out what are the right songs to go with for it. What people do with them is so fascinating.”
p

Preluding the climax of the film, Jimmy serenades his family at his parents’ 50th wedding anniversary with a harrowingly raw rendition of Melanie’s “Look What They Did to My Song, Ma.” In this emotionally intense moment, Jimmy’s performance is just as much a confessional as his nephew’s recording of a video on a camcorder during which Jimmy unburdens intense guilt over the life he’s led. The quivering and change in tone of Jimmy’s singing, from beginning to end, brings us on the same emotional journey and realization of helplessness that Jimmy goes through in this moment. Lyrically, “Look What They Did to My Song, Ma” deals with an artist’s loss of control over their art. In Melanie’s case, commercialization was the enemy encroaching on her creative expression; yet we, along with Jimmy, realize this sense of artistic erosion is applicable to his life, as his illness slowly hinders his cognitive abilities, in turn holding him back from inhabiting the very space that makes him feel most alive.
p

Asked “Why Gershwin?,” during the Q&A, Sachs invoked noir melodrama “The Man I Love” (1947) by replying, “Well, why Raoul Walsh?” Sachs drew additional inspiration from other films and television: “I was really watching, or rediscovering again, a film called Van Gogh by Maurice Pialat, which is about the last four months of Van Gogh’s life,” Sachs told us. “It’s [about] a man who’s facing mortality but at the same time he’s having an affair, and he’s painting, and going out to clubs—it’s the Moulin Rouge but he’s going—so we were like, ‘That’s a really good structure for the film we’re interested in making.’”
p

Sachs additionally credited the Claire Denis film “Beau Travail” as an influence and discussed another lesser-known inspiration on the scene of Jimmy’s camcorder address. “The confession Jimmy makes with his nephew is actually a direct lift, credited to a film, [“Confessions”], made in 1972 by Curt McDowell, an experimental gay filmmaker in San Francisco who died of AIDS,” Sachs said. “Throughout the film, there is this sense of welcoming my relationship to cinema, which I think has been a big part of the work I have done lately.”
p

Sachs’s film, as a whole, operates as a beautiful patchwork, paying homage to an assortment of personal inspirations which found their way into his newest creation. The intentional mirroring of other films relating to the plot of his own created layers of artistic performance for the actors to play around with; condensed into one finite context, these echoes of past queer films reflect a depth of understanding within Sachs’ character portrait. His soundtrack and score choices additionally build to the film’s poignant, intensely cinematic climax, in which Jimmy’s illness fully undermines him on stage, rendering him incapable of performing the one last number he had been striving toward prior to the film’s beginning. But despite such tragic notes, “The Man I Love” feels still beautifully personal, recalling all of life’s sensory pleasures as it explores how a queer performer in the 1980s expressed these delights on humanity’s behalf.
